newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to import record 8.9 mln bpd petroleum in '97.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to import record 8.9 mln bpd petroleum in '97.

text.p: The United States is expected to import 8.9 million barrels per day of crude oil and refined products in 1997, topping a 20-year-old record of 8.6 million bpd, the Energy Information Administration said Friday.

Net crude imports alone should climb to 7.76 million bpd this year, up 4.7 percent from 1996 but down from a previous forecast of 7.83 million bpd for 1997, EIA said in its "Short-Term Energy Outlook".
It saw net products imports for 1997 at 1.15 million bpd, up 160,000 bpd from last year, and up 90,000 bpd from a previous projection for 1997.
EIA raised its outlook for imported crude prices in 1997 to $21.04 per barrel from a previous forecast of $19.18 in nominal dollars, even with Iraqi oil on the market.
"Prices in 1997 are assumed to be at their highest in the first quarter at $21.80 per barrel, as low stocks coupled with winter demand will absorb the additional Iraqi oil," EIA said.
If Iraq had not resumed some exports, EIA said its forecast for oil prices would have been $1 to $2 higher.
Imported oil prices in 1996 at an estimated average of $20.57 were $0.67 higher than EIA projected earlier. In the last quarter alone, prices were $2.75 higher than expected.
EIA projected U.S. oil production would fall 2 percent in 1997 to 6.35 million barrels per day, hiking its previous outlook for 1997 by 30,000 bpd.
Total petroleum demand in 1997 was expected to reach 18.36 million bpd up from an estimated 18.23 million bpd in 1996 and an earlier projection of 18.31 million bpd for 1997.
Gasoline demand should rise 2.0 percent to 8.01 million bpd in 1997 from last year.
EIA predicted gasoline pump prices would not climb as much during the 1997 driving season as they did in 1996 because prices were already starting high.

"However, the same combination of factors that caused gasoline prices to jump in the second quarter of each of the previous two years is expected to be in effect in 1998, but on a smaller scale," EIA said.
Retail gasoline prices should average $1.32 in 1997, up 3 cents from 1996, and up 4 cents from a previous projection.
Demand for jet fuel was expected to increase 1.3 percent to 1.61 million bpd from last year, up from a previous forecast of 1.59 million bpd for 1997.
Distillate demand in 1997 was projected to climb 2.7 percent from last year to 3.46 million bpd, up from an earlier projection of 3.34 million bpd.
EIA pegged residual fuel demand in 1997 at 890,000 bpd, up 4.7 percent from 1996 and up from a previous forecast of 870,000 bpd.
The outlook assumed that U.S. gross domestic product would rise 2.2 percent and weather patterns would be normal in 1997.
